To further validate the neural network prediction outcomes, we investigated the influence of the input dataset on the prediction error. We obtain the dataset following a near-gaussian distribution with all the 220-sample data (with each data representing one solar cell pixel). As shown in Fig.7.5a, we statistically group all those data based on their PCE into 8 groups. The three photovoltaic parameters are also simultaneously categorized into 8 groups. With an increasing number of data shown in the training input, the prediction accuracy corresponding to that group tends to increase. An averaged percent error from Fig. 7.5a is replotted in Fig. 7.5b. for Voc, Jsc, and FF individually. As shown in the distribution, with an increasing number of data points within the whole input, an enhancement in accuracy is achieved and finally reaches below 5% error. It is interesting to note that when the number of data points within the whole dataset increases to a Page 41 of 54 DE-EE0009512 Massachusetts Institute of Technology number around 45 which is around 20% of all the data points, the accuracy reaches above 95%. Among the three prediction values, FF tends to have the largest prediction fluctuations compared with the other two outputs as FF is not perfectly reflected by the optical properties. The input training dataset to test dataset ratio follows: 210:10, 200:20, 70:150, 110:110, 75:145, 55:165, 36:184, 20:200. To test the threshold cases in predicting a large number of different cells, we have carried out the “pressure test” to the algorithm by largely decreasing the amount of data in the training dataset while increasing the number of data we are planning to predict in the validation dataset. For a normal ratio between validation datasets and prediction datasets, the validation datasets generally take around 5%-10% of the number of samples in the training dataset. Hence, in our general cases, we choose to use 210 data as the training dataset and the rest 10 data as validation. However, as for the pressure test, we increased the ratio of validation to training from 5% to 1000%, i.e., 10 times more data in the validation dataset compared to the training data. As shown in Fig. 7.5c, an increasing averaged percent error is observed with the increasing validation-to- train ratio reaching around 50%.
